rule: Never draw or name a product in a form it does not take: read its product file (container, colour, proportion, how it is held) before any brief or picture
why: a tube was briefed and drawn as a jar in every Black Friday picture

rule: A moment email (a holiday, a sale weekend) opens on a blow-out key visual: a borrowed format at full scale (flyer front page, movie or TV title card, magazine cover, gift reveal) with the real product as its star
why: the first Black Friday emails were quiet kitchen snapshots in a dark frame

rule: Research the moment from the reader's side first (what she is actually doing, buying and watching that week) and build every concept and made picture from it
why: Black Friday read like any other week until her weekend was researched

rule: Every person in an email is a real one from the brand's tagged index (real customers holding the real product) before any made person; make only the key visual and the gift pictures
why: the owner: use real people, use real content

rule: Use the brand's own signature elements from its visual DNA in every email (its crest, its signature product shot, its ingredient cards, its real customers): a reader should know the brand with the logo covered
why: a brand's emails had no branded elements

rule: Never two emails in one batch on the same concept
why: two Black Friday emails both came back as a recipe card

rule: Clean sections: 8 to 11, one idea each, never two text-only sections in a row, one alignment, one button style, short words
why: the owner: use clean sections, you are an expert designer

rule: Never judge or show a render that is not at true 400px phone width: headless Chrome renders at 500px, so crop the left 400
why: every Black Friday preview was cut off on the right

rule: Never write a sale, a price or a deadline the offer bank does not hold for that send
why: a brand's Black Friday copy invented 'ends Monday' and a 'Black Friday price'

rule: Never hand-cut a chain-written script to fit a format. Size the story to the format first: the word limit and the clip limit go into the story before writing, and the chain writes to them.
A series part is written from what the earlier part shows on screen (its finished cut: the shots, the lines heard, the props seen), never from the earlier part's script.
Name the product in the setup line. No character reacts to a product they could not know about yet; the line that brings it in says what it is by name.
No flashback in a micro drama: time only moves forward.
Never send a multi-view product sheet (the seven-view turnaround) as a clip reference next to a teen's face: the clip model flags it. Send one front view cropped from the approved sheet.

Production keeps the earlier part's full reference set for every character: the face sheet, the outfit sheet, the camera-movement clip, and the acting written shot by shot. A mechanical check that prints PASS is not quality; the take is judged on how it looks.
Only a price quote stops a run for the owner. Every other call is made by the run and filed through the decision layer.
Every correction the owner makes is saved as a learning and handed to the next run; a run never starts from less than the last one knew.
